If you have been following along with this series, you know the plan: build a conference badge that listens for a wake word, transcribes what you say, and uses an on-device LLM to generate a response. Simple enough on paper. But here is the thing about embedded systems - the paper lies to you.

This post is about what happens when your carefully architected Plan A crashes into the brick wall of physical constraints. And more importantly, how we invented a workaround that ended up being kind of brilliant. Well, at least I think so. You can judge for yourself.

## The STT Problem - When 8MB Is Not Enough

The original architecture was elegant in its simplicity:

```
Wake Word → Speech-to-Text → LLM → TTS
```

The user says "Hey Daisy," the badge wakes up, transcribes their question using STT, sends it to the LLM, and speaks the response. Clean. Logical. Completely impossible.

See, I had done my research on the LLM side. I knew we needed about 6MB of our 8MB PSRAM for the Q8_0 quantized language model. That leaves 2MB for everything else - video buffers, audio buffers, the works. Tight, but doable with careful memory management.

Then I started looking at STT models.

{{< sub-section title="The Model Size Reality Check" icon="fa-weight-hanging" >}}
- **Whisper tiny**: 75MB+ (the "tiny" is apparently ironic)
- **Whisper base**: 150MB+
- **wav2vec2-base**: 100MB+
- **Distilled variants**: 30-50MB (still laughable for our use case)
- **Our available memory**: 2MB (generous estimate)

Even the most aggressively distilled, quantized, pruned STT models I could find were an order of magnitude too large. And these are the "edge-optimized" ones that papers brag about running on mobile devices. A mobile device with 8GB of RAM, sure. Not quite the same as 8MB of PSRAM shared with an LLM.
{{< /sub-section >}}

I spent a solid week trying to make STT work. Maybe we could stream chunks? No, the models need context. What about a much smaller vocabulary? Still too big. What if we just transcribe single words? That is called keyword spotting, and we already have wake word detection.

This was the "oh crap" moment. The architecture I had been building toward for weeks was fundamentally impossible. Not hard. Not expensive. Impossible.

## The Pivot - If You Cannot Transcribe, Match

I was sitting there, staring at the dataset we had prepared - 2,008 questions that conference attendees might ask about me, the schedule, booth locations, that sort of thing. And it hit me:

Why do we need to transcribe at all?

Think about it. We have a finite, known set of questions. We are not building a general-purpose voice assistant. This is a conference badge. People will ask things like "What is your email?" or "Where is the keynote?" - questions we can anticipate.

What if, instead of:
```
Audio → Text → Match to Intent
```

We did:
```
Audio → Embedding → Match to Pre-embedded Intents
```

Skip the text entirely. Train a model to map spoken audio directly to the same embedding space as our question texts. Then similarity search finds the closest match.

{{< sub-section title="The Trade-off" icon="fa-balance-scale" >}}
This approach trades flexibility for efficiency:
- **Cannot handle arbitrary questions** - only matches to known intents
- **Needs training data for each intent** - cannot generalize to new questions
- **But fits in ~300KB** instead of 75MB+
- **Perfect for our use case** - we know exactly what questions are possible

For a general voice assistant, this would be a non-starter. For a conference badge with a defined set of FAQs? It is actually better than STT in some ways - it directly maps to intents without parsing text.
{{< /sub-section >}}

The new architecture became:

```
Wake Word → Record 3s → Audio Embedding → Similarity Search → LLM (if match) → TTS
```

If the similarity score is high enough (we settled on 0.7), we treat it as a match and feed the corresponding question to the LLM. If not, the badge apologizes and stashes the audio for later analysis. This way we can discover what questions people are actually asking that we had not anticipated.

## Contrastive Learning - Teaching Audio and Text to Speak the Same Language

The core idea is to train two neural networks - one for audio, one for text - that map their respective inputs to the same 256-dimensional embedding space. When you say "What is your email address?" the audio embedding should be close to the text embedding of that same question.

This is contrastive learning, and it is the same fundamental approach that powers things like CLIP (images and text) and audio-language models. The key insight is that you do not need to explicitly transcribe - you just need the representations to align.

{{< sub-section title="The Two-Tower Architecture" icon="fa-building" >}}
**Audio Branch:**
- Input: YAMNet features (1024-dim) or mel-spectrogram (64×96)
- BatchNormalization
- Dense(512, relu)
- Dropout(0.2)
- Dense(256)
- L2 Normalize
- Output: 256-dim embedding

**Text Branch:**
- Input: MPNet embeddings (768-dim)
- BatchNormalization
- Dense(256)
- L2 Normalize
- Output: 256-dim embedding
{{< /sub-section >}}

Think of it like GPS coordinates. Audio and text are two completely different things - one is a waveform, the other is symbols. But we can train both branches to output "coordinates" in the same space. If someone asks "What is your email?" in audio, and we have the text "What is your email?" pre-embedded, they should end up at nearly the same coordinates.

The contrastive loss function is elegant:

```python
class ContrastiveLoss(tf.keras.losses.Loss):
    def __init__(self, temperature=0.2, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.temperature = temperature
    
    def call(self, audio_emb, text_emb):
        # Compute similarity matrix (audio × text)
        logits = tf.matmul(audio_emb, text_emb, transpose_b=True) / self.temperature
        batch_size = tf.shape(audio_emb)[0]
        labels = tf.range(batch_size)  # Diagonal should be highest
        
        # Cross-entropy in both directions
        loss_a2t = tf.nn.sparse_softmax_cross_entropy_with_logits(labels=labels, logits=logits)
        loss_t2a = tf.nn.sparse_softmax_cross_entropy_with_logits(labels=labels, logits=tf.transpose(logits))
        
        return (tf.reduce_mean(loss_a2t) + tf.reduce_mean(loss_t2a)) / 2
```

The temperature parameter controls how "sharp" the similarity distribution is. Lower temperature = more confident predictions but harder to train. We used 0.2 which worked well for our dataset size.

## The Bucketed Batch Sampling Innovation - This Was the Breakthrough

Here is where things got interesting. After initial training, our model was achieving about 4% accuracy. Four percent. Basically random chance.

I spent days debugging. Was the audio quality bad? Was the model too small? Were we overfitting? I tried everything - more layers, fewer layers, different learning rates, longer training. Nothing worked.

Then I visualized what the model was actually learning.

It was learning to distinguish speakers.

{{< sub-section title="The Problem with Naive Batching" icon="fa-exclamation-triangle" >}}
With standard batch sampling, a batch might contain:
- "What is your email?" - Speaker 1, Male, US accent
- "What is your email?" - Speaker 2, Female, UK accent
- "What is your email?" - Speaker 1, Male, US accent (augmented)
- "Where is the keynote?" - Speaker 3, Female, US accent

The easiest way to tell samples 1-3 apart from sample 4 is not the semantic content - it is the speaker characteristics! The model learned "this sounds like a male voice" vs "this sounds like a female voice" instead of "this is asking about email" vs "this is asking about location."
{{< /sub-section >}}

The solution was semantic bucketing. We cluster all 2,008 questions by their text similarity using MPNet embeddings:

```python
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering

# Questions above 0.85 similarity go in the same bucket
distance_threshold = 1 - 0.85  # Convert similarity to distance
clustering = AgglomerativeClustering(
    n_clusters=None,
    distance_threshold=distance_threshold,
    metric='cosine',
    linkage='average'
)
cluster_labels = clustering.fit_predict(question_embeddings)
```

This gave us 1,698 buckets from 2,008 questions. Semantically similar questions like "What is your email address?" and "Tell me your contact email" end up in the same bucket.

Now here is the key: during training, each batch contains exactly ONE sample per bucket. If bucket 149 contains both "What is your email address?" and "Tell me your contact email," we only pick one of them for any given batch.

```python
class BucketedBatchGenerator:
    def generate_batch(self):
        # Randomly select batch_size buckets
        selected_buckets = random.sample(self.all_buckets, self.batch_size)
        
        batch_audio, batch_text = [], []
        for bucket_id in selected_buckets:
            # ONE sample per bucket - forces semantic distinction
            idx = random.choice(self.bucket_to_indices[bucket_id])
            batch_audio.append(self.audio_embs[idx])
            batch_text.append(self.text_embs[idx])
        
        return np.array(batch_audio), np.array(batch_text)
```

This forces the model to distinguish between semantically different questions, not just different speakers saying the same thing.

The accuracy jump was immediate: 4% to 70-90% bucket matching accuracy. The model was finally learning what we wanted it to learn.

## Multi-GPU Dataset Generation - Scaling to 32,128 Samples

Training an audio embedding model needs audio. Lots of audio. And not just any audio - we needed multiple speakers saying each of our 2,008 questions with various augmentations.

The math:
- 2,008 questions
- 8 different voices (TED speaker samples)
- 2 variants per recording (original + augmented)
- = 32,128 audio samples

Generating this with XTTS-v2 on a single GPU would take forever. So we rented 12 RTX 4070 SUPERs on vast.ai and parallelized everything.

{{< sub-section title="Why XTTS-v2 and Not gTTS?" icon="fa-microphone" >}}
We initially tried Google's gTTS (text-to-speech). It is free, fast, and easy. The resulting model achieved 4% accuracy.

The problem? gTTS produces robotic, synthetic speech that sounds nothing like how real humans talk. YAMNet (our audio feature extractor) was trained on real human speech, podcasts, conversations. When we fed it gTTS audio, the features were garbage.

XTTS-v2 does voice cloning - you give it a 6-second sample of a speaker, and it synthesizes new speech in their voice. The output sounds like actual human speech with natural prosody, hesitations, and rhythm. YAMNet features from XTTS audio were dramatically better.

Accuracy jumped from 4% (gTTS) to 70%+ (XTTS-v2). The quality of synthetic training data matters enormously.
{{< /sub-section >}}

The parallelization strategy was straightforward but had some tricks:

```python
def gpu_worker(args):
    worker_id, data = args
    
    # Assign this worker to specific GPU
    os.environ['CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES'] = str(worker_id)
    
    # Calculate question range for this worker
    questions_per_worker = len(questions) // num_gpus
    start_idx = worker_id * questions_per_worker
    end_idx = start_idx + questions_per_worker if worker_id < num_gpus - 1 else len(questions)
    
    # Load XTTS on this GPU (each worker has its own model instance)
    tts = TTS("tts_models/multilingual/multi-dataset/xtts_v2").to("cuda")
    
    # Pre-compute speaker latents - this was the bottleneck!
    speaker_latents = {}
    for speaker_file in speaker_files:
        gpt_cond_latent, speaker_embedding = tts.synthesizer.tts_model.get_conditioning_latents(
            audio_path=speaker_file
        )
        speaker_latents[speaker_file] = (gpt_cond_latent, speaker_embedding)
```

The speaker latent pre-computation was critical. XTTS needs to analyze the reference speaker audio before synthesizing - doing this per-sample was killing performance. By computing it once per speaker at worker startup, we got a 3x speedup.

We also added JSON checkpoint files so workers could resume if something crashed:

```python
def save_generation_state(worker_id, question_idx, speaker_idx, total_generated):
    state = {
        'worker_id': worker_id,
        'question_idx': question_idx,
        'speaker_idx': speaker_idx,
        'total_generated': total_generated,
        'timestamp': datetime.now().isoformat()
    }
    with open(get_state_file(worker_id), 'w') as f:
        json.dump(state, f)
```

Total generation time: about 4 hours for 32,128 samples across 12 GPUs. Not bad for a dataset that would have taken 2 days on a single GPU.

## ESP32-Optimized CNN Encoder - Shrinking YAMNet

YAMNet is great for extracting audio features, but it is 3.5MB - way too big for our memory budget. We needed a tiny model that takes mel-spectrograms directly and outputs 256-dim embeddings.

The architecture is deliberately minimal:

```python
def build_audio_encoder():
    inputs = tf.keras.Input(shape=(64, 96, 1))  # Mel-spectrogram
    
    # Conv blocks with aggressive pooling
    x = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(32, 3, padding='same', activation='relu')(inputs)
    x = tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(2)(x)  # 32×48
    
    x = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(64, 3, padding='same', activation='relu')(x)
    x = tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(2)(x)  # 16×24
    
    x = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(128, 3, padding='same', activation='relu')(x)
    x = tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(2)(x)  # 8×12
    
    x = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(128, 3, padding='same', activation='relu')(x)
    x = tf.keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)  # 128-dim
    
    # Project to embedding
    x = tf.keras.layers.Dense(256)(x)
    outputs = tf.keras.layers.Lambda(lambda x: tf.nn.l2_normalize(x, axis=1))(x)
    
    return tf.keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
```

This gives us about 273KB of parameters. After int8 quantization, the TFLite model is around 288KB - small enough to coexist with our LLM.

Input specification:
- 64 mel bins (covering 125Hz to 7500Hz)
- 96 frames (about 1.5 seconds of audio at 10ms hop)
- Single channel

The model is trained with the same contrastive loss, but now it learns to go directly from mel-spectrograms to the shared embedding space, without needing YAMNet as an intermediate feature extractor.

## Mel-Spectrogram Generation with ESP-DSP

Computing mel-spectrograms on the ESP32-S3 requires careful optimization. We use ESP-DSP for the heavy lifting - it provides SIMD-accelerated FFT and dot products that are 5-10x faster than naive implementations.

```cpp
bool AudioEmbedder::_computeMelSpectrogram(const int16_t* audio, size_t samples, float* melOutput) {
    float globalMin = 1e10f, globalMax = -1e10f;
    
    for (int frame = 0; frame < AUDIO_MEL_FRAMES; frame++) {
        int startIdx = frame * AUDIO_HOP_LENGTH;
        
        // Compute power spectrum for this frame
        float powerSpectrum[AUDIO_FFT_SIZE / 2 + 1];
        _computeFFTFrame(audio, startIdx, powerSpectrum);
        
        // Apply mel filterbank (SIMD-accelerated)
        float melFrame[AUDIO_MEL_BINS];
        _applyMelFilterbank(powerSpectrum, melFrame);
        
        // Store in (bins, frames) format for CNN input
        for (int i = 0; i < AUDIO_MEL_BINS; i++) {
            melOutput[i * AUDIO_MEL_FRAMES + frame] = melFrame[i];
            if (melFrame[i] < globalMin) globalMin = melFrame[i];
            if (melFrame[i] > globalMax) globalMax = melFrame[i];
        }
    }
    
    // Normalize to [0, 1] - critical for matching training preprocessing
    float range = globalMax - globalMin;
    if (range > 1e-8f) {
        for (int i = 0; i < AUDIO_MEL_BINS * AUDIO_MEL_FRAMES; i++) {
            melOutput[i] = (melOutput[i] - globalMin) / range;
        }
    }
    return true;
}
```

The FFT is where ESP-DSP shines:

```cpp
void AudioEmbedder::_computeFFTFrame(const int16_t* audio, int startIdx, float* powerSpectrum) {
    // Apply Hann window and convert to float
    for (int i = 0; i < AUDIO_FFT_SIZE; i++) {
        _fftInput[i] = (float)audio[startIdx + i] * _window[i] / 32768.0f;
    }
    
    // Prepare complex input
    for (int i = 0; i < AUDIO_FFT_SIZE; i++) {
        _fftOutput[i * 2] = _fftInput[i];      // Real
        _fftOutput[i * 2 + 1] = 0.0f;           // Imaginary
    }
    
    // ESP-DSP accelerated FFT
    dsps_fft2r_fc32(_fftOutput, AUDIO_FFT_SIZE);
    dsps_bit_rev_fc32(_fftOutput, AUDIO_FFT_SIZE);
    
    // Compute power spectrum
    for (int k = 0; k < AUDIO_FFT_SIZE / 2 + 1; k++) {
        float real = _fftOutput[k * 2];
        float imag = _fftOutput[k * 2 + 1];
        powerSpectrum[k] = real * real + imag * imag;
    }
}
```

The mel filterbank application is also SIMD-accelerated:

```cpp
void AudioEmbedder::_applyMelFilterbank(float* powerSpectrum, float* melOutput) {
    int numFreqBins = AUDIO_FFT_SIZE / 2 + 1;
    
    for (int m = 0; m < AUDIO_MEL_BINS; m++) {
        float sum = 0.0f;
        // ESP-DSP SIMD dot product
        dsps_dotprod_f32_aes3(&_melFilterbank[m * numFreqBins], 
                              powerSpectrum, &sum, numFreqBins);
        melOutput[m] = log10f(sum + 1e-10f);  // Log transform
    }
}
```

The Hann window and mel filterbank are precomputed at initialization and stored in PSRAM (with 16-byte alignment for SIMD). This way the per-frame computation is just FFT + matrix-vector multiply + log.

## SIMD-Accelerated Similarity Search

Once we have the audio embedding, we need to find the closest match among our pre-embedded intents. This is a linear search through 256 embeddings, computing cosine similarity for each.

Without optimization, this would be painfully slow. With ESP-DSP's SIMD instructions, it is about 100ms for the entire search.

```cpp
float EmbeddingSearch::_cosineSimilarity(const float* a, const float* b) {
    float dot = 0.0f;
    float normA = 0.0f;
    float normB = 0.0f;
    
    // ESP-DSP SIMD dot products - 5-10x faster than scalar
    // Uses PIE (Processor Instruction Extensions) on ESP32-S3
    dsps_dotprod_f32_aes3(a, b, &dot, AUDIO_EMBEDDING_DIM);
    dsps_dotprod_f32_aes3(a, a, &normA, AUDIO_EMBEDDING_DIM);
    dsps_dotprod_f32_aes3(b, b, &normB, AUDIO_EMBEDDING_DIM);
    
    float denom = sqrtf(normA) * sqrtf(normB);
    return (denom > 1e-8f) ? dot / denom : 0.0f;
}
```

The search function tracks the top 5 matches for debugging purposes:

```cpp
SearchResult EmbeddingSearch::search(const float* embedding) {
    const int TOP_K = 5;
    float topScores[TOP_K] = {-1, -1, -1, -1, -1};
    int topIndices[TOP_K] = {-1, -1, -1, -1, -1};
    
    for (int i = 0; i < _count; i++) {
        float score = _cosineSimilarity(embedding, &_embeddings[i * AUDIO_EMBEDDING_DIM]);
        
        // Insertion sort into top-K
        if (score > topScores[TOP_K - 1]) {
            int insertAt = TOP_K - 1;
            while (insertAt > 0 && score > topScores[insertAt - 1]) {
                topScores[insertAt] = topScores[insertAt - 1];
                topIndices[insertAt] = topIndices[insertAt - 1];
                insertAt--;
            }
            topScores[insertAt] = score;
            topIndices[insertAt] = i;
        }
    }
    
    // Return best match
    SearchResult result;
    result.intentIdx = topIndices[0];
    result.score = topScores[0];
    _getIntent(topIndices[0], result.intent, sizeof(result.intent));
    return result;
}
```

The intent lookup is O(1) thanks to a precomputed offset table:

```cpp
void EmbeddingSearch::_getIntent(int idx, char* buffer, size_t bufSize) {
    // _intentOffsets[idx] points directly to the start of intent string
    const char* intentStr = _intentsData + _intentOffsets[idx];
    strncpy(buffer, intentStr, bufSize - 1);
    buffer[bufSize - 1] = '\0';
}
```

Memory layout for the embedding database:
- 256 embeddings x 256 dimensions x 4 bytes = 262KB
- Stored in PSRAM with 16-byte alignment for SIMD

## Results and Timing

After all the optimization, here is what we achieved:

| Operation | Time |
|-----------|------|
| Mel-spectrogram extraction | ~80ms |
| CNN inference | ~120ms |
| Similarity search (256 embeddings) | ~100ms |
| **Total audio-to-intent** | **~300ms** |

Not bad for a $15 microcontroller.

{{< sub-section title="What Worked" icon="fa-check-circle" >}}
- **Bucketed batch sampling** - The single biggest accuracy improvement
- **XTTS-v2 instead of gTTS** - Realistic speech dramatically improved YAMNet features
- **ESP-DSP SIMD** - 5-10x speedup on math operations
- **Pre-computed filterbanks and windows** - No per-frame allocation
- **Offset-based intent lookup** - O(1) string retrieval
{{< /sub-section >}}

{{< sub-section title="What Did Not Work" icon="fa-times-circle" >}}
- **YAMNet on ESP32** - At 3.5MB, too big. Had to train our own tiny encoder.
- **Standard batch sampling** - Model learned speaker characteristics instead of semantics
- **gTTS for training data** - Robotic speech produced garbage features
- **Single-GPU training data generation** - Would have taken days instead of hours
{{< /sub-section >}}

Would I do this again? Absolutely. The audio embedding approach is actually more elegant than STT for our use case. We bypass the entire text domain and match directly to intents. The only limitation is that we cannot handle arbitrary questions - but for a conference badge with known FAQs, that is not a limitation at all.

If anything, this project reinforced something I keep learning in embedded systems: constraints force creativity. We could not fit STT, so we invented something better suited to our actual problem. Sometimes Plan B is not just a backup - it is the answer you should have started with.

## The Quest for Speed on a Microcontroller

So here we are at Blog 5, and this is the one I have been itching to write. If Blog 2 was about getting a transformer to run on an ESP32, this one is about making it actually useful. The previous post covered basic float32 inference with ESP-DSP SIMD - and yeah, it worked, but let me be honest, it was painfully slow. We are talking about a model that took forever to generate tokens, eating up way more memory than we could afford.

This blog covers what changed: Q8_0 quantization shrinking the model 4x, inline ESP32-S3 PIE assembly achieving 16 int8 MACs per cycle, and a three-phase training pipeline that taught a 6MB model to answer 2,008 questions about a specific person. The result? A personalized Q&A bot running entirely on-device with a robot voice. Sounds stupid right? Let me show you how stupid can be beautiful.

The journey from "it runs" to "it runs well" required diving deep into the ESP32-S3's undocumented vector unit - something I had zero experience with before this project. With heavy Claude Code assistance (I am not an expert in assembly, let me be clear), we managed to squeeze out performance that I honestly did not think was possible on a $10 microcontroller.

---

## What Changed Since Last Time

In Blog 2, we got a basic llama2.c port running on the ESP32-S3. That implementation used:

- **Float32 weights**: Every single parameter stored as a 4-byte float
- **ESP-DSP SIMD**: Using `dsps_dotprod_f32_aes3()` for vectorized float operations
- **Dual-core parallelism**: Splitting matmul across both cores with FreeRTOS tasks
- **Stories15M model**: A 15M parameter model trained on TinyStories

It worked. But "works" and "usable" are different things. The float32 model ate almost all our PSRAM, leaving barely enough room for the KV cache. Generation speed was around 1-2 tokens per second at best - fine for a demo, but not for an interactive badge experience.

The new implementation changes everything:

- **Q8_0 quantization**: 8-bit integer weights with float32 scales per group
- **PIE assembly**: Custom inline assembly hitting 16 MACs per CPU cycle
- **Single-core simplicity**: Turns out the overhead of dual-core coordination was not worth it for our model sizes
- **Fine-tuned 6M model**: Custom-trained to answer specific questions about a person

The performance difference? We went from roughly 0.5 tokens/second to 1.2-1.5 tokens/second with 4x less memory usage. Not exactly GPT-4 speeds, but for a conference badge that speaks robot TTS? Perfectly acceptable.

## Q8_0 Quantization Deep Dive

{{< sub-section title="What is Q8_0 Anyway?" icon="fa-compress" >}}
Q8_0 is one of the simplest quantization formats from the llama.cpp ecosystem. The "Q8" means 8-bit integers, and the "0" means no additional bits for fine-grained scaling (unlike Q4_K or Q5_K formats which have per-block super-scales). It is the highest-fidelity integer format before you just store floats.

The core idea: instead of storing each weight as a 4-byte float, we store it as a 1-byte signed integer (-128 to 127) plus one shared scale factor per group of weights. This scale tells us how to convert back to the approximate float value.
{{< /sub-section >}}

### Per-Group Scaling

The key insight is that weights in neural networks tend to cluster around similar magnitudes within local regions. So instead of having one global scale for all millions of parameters (which would destroy precision), we compute a scale for every 32 or 64 weights. This is called the "group size" (GS).

Here is how quantization works mathematically:

```cpp
// For each group of GS weights:
float max_abs = find_max_absolute_value(group);
float scale = max_abs / 127.0f;  // 127 is max positive int8

// Quantize each weight in the group
for (int i = 0; i < GS; i++) {
    int8_t quantized = round(weight[i] / scale);
    // quantized now fits in [-127, 127]
}
```

And to dequantize (convert back to float):
```cpp
float dequantized = quantized_value * scale;
```

The magic is that we never actually dequantize during inference. We do the multiply-accumulate in int8, then multiply by both scales only once at the end of each group. This keeps the inner loop blazing fast.

### Memory Layout

In the Q8_0 format, each group of 64 weights is stored as:
- 64 bytes of int8 values (the quantized weights)
- 4 bytes for the float32 scale

So for 64 weights, we use 68 bytes instead of 256 bytes (64 x 4). That is about 3.76x compression. In practice, with the model header and scale overhead, our 6M parameter model shrinks from 21.26 MB (float32) to 5.98 MB (Q8_0).

Here is the actual quantization code from our implementation:

```cpp
void quantize(QuantizedTensor *qx, float* x, int n) {
    int num_groups = n / GS;
    float Q_MAX = 127.0f;

    for (int group = 0; group < num_groups; group++) {
        float* gx = x + group * GS;
        int8_t* gq = qx->q + group * GS;

        // Find max absolute value (unrolled for pipelining)
        float wmax = 0.0f;
        for (int i = 0; i < GS; i += 4) {
            float v0 = fabsf(gx[i]);
            float v1 = fabsf(gx[i+1]);
            float v2 = fabsf(gx[i+2]);
            float v3 = fabsf(gx[i+3]);
            if (v0 > wmax) wmax = v0;
            if (v1 > wmax) wmax = v1;
            if (v2 > wmax) wmax = v2;
            if (v3 > wmax) wmax = v3;
        }

        float scale = wmax / Q_MAX;
        qx->s[group] = scale;

        // Quantize with reciprocal multiply (faster than division)
        float inv_scale = (scale > 1e-10f) ? Q_MAX / wmax : 0.0f;
        for (int i = 0; i < GS; i += 4) {
            gq[i]   = (int8_t)(gx[i]   * inv_scale + 0.5f - (gx[i]   < 0));
            gq[i+1] = (int8_t)(gx[i+1] * inv_scale + 0.5f - (gx[i+1] < 0));
            gq[i+2] = (int8_t)(gx[i+2] * inv_scale + 0.5f - (gx[i+2] < 0));
            gq[i+3] = (int8_t)(gx[i+3] * inv_scale + 0.5f - (gx[i+3] < 0));
        }
    }
}
```

Notice the manual loop unrolling (processing 4 values at a time). This helps the CPU pipeline instructions better - while one multiply is executing, the next one is being fetched. Little optimizations like this add up when you are doing millions of operations.

### Quantization Error Tracking

When exporting the model from PyTorch, the training script tracks the maximum quantization error per layer:

```
57/57 quantized (768, 224) to Q8_0 with max error 0.0006260164082050323
max quantization group error across all weights: 0.002027716487646103
```

That max error of 0.002 means our worst-case weight reconstruction error is about 0.2% - negligible for inference quality, but massive for memory savings.

## ESP32-S3 PIE Vector Unit

{{< sub-section title="What is PIE?" icon="fa-microchip" >}}
PIE stands for "Processing Instructions Extensions" - Espressif's name for the vector/SIMD unit in the ESP32-S3. Unlike the basic ESP32, the S3 variant includes a 128-bit vector unit that can process 16 int8 values simultaneously. This is the same chip feature that enables fast audio processing and computer vision - and we are hijacking it for LLM inference.
{{< /sub-section >}}

The ESP32-S3 PIE unit gives us:

- **128-bit vector registers**: q0 through q7, each holding 16 int8 values
- **40-bit accumulator**: accx_0 (low 32 bits) and accx_1 (high 8 bits) for overflow-safe accumulation
- **Vector load with auto-increment**: `ee.vld.128.ip` loads 16 bytes and advances the pointer
- **Fused multiply-accumulate**: `ee.vmulas.s8.accx` does 16 MACs in a single instruction
- **Zero-overhead hardware loops**: `loopnez` eliminates loop counter overhead

### The Key Instructions

Let me break down the PIE instructions we use:

**`ee.vld.128.ip q0, %[ptr], 16`**
- Load 128 bits (16 bytes) from memory address in `%[ptr]`
- Store them in vector register q0
- Auto-increment the pointer by 16 bytes
- "ip" means "immediate post-increment"

**`ee.vmulas.s8.accx q0, q1`**
- Multiply corresponding elements of q0 and q1 (16 pairs of int8)
- Accumulate all 16 products into the 40-bit accumulator
- The "s8" means signed 8-bit, "accx" means use the extended accumulator

**`wur.accx_0 %[zero]`**
- Write a value to the accumulator's low 32 bits
- "wur" stands for "write user register"
- We use this to clear the accumulator before starting

**`rur.accx_0 %[result]`**
- Read the accumulator's low 32 bits into a general-purpose register
- "rur" stands for "read user register"

**`loopnez %[count], label`**
- Hardware loop that executes until count reaches zero
- Zero-overhead: no branch prediction misses, no counter decrement instructions
- Incredibly efficient for tight inner loops

### Why 40-bit Accumulator Matters

Here is a quick overflow calculation. Each int8 multiply can produce at most:
```
127 * 127 = 16,129 (fits in 15 bits)
```

In one `vmulas` instruction, we add 16 such products:
```
16 * 16,129 = 258,064 (fits in 18 bits)
```

For a typical layer dimension of 224, we have 224/16 = 14 loop iterations:
```
14 * 258,064 = 3,612,896 (fits in 22 bits)
```

But for larger dimensions like hidden_dim=896:
```
(896/16) * 258,064 = 14,451,584 (25 bits)
```

And if we chain multiple groups? A 32-bit accumulator could overflow. The 40-bit accumulator gives us headroom up to 1 trillion - more than enough for any reasonable layer size. This is crucial because checking for overflow would destroy our performance.

---

## THE PIE ASSEMBLY MATMUL - The Heart of Inference

This is it. The single most performance-critical function in the entire codebase. Every token generation requires hundreds of matrix multiplications, and each one calls this function for every output element:

```cpp
// PIE SIMD int8 dot product - returns full int32 accumulator
// Processes 16 int8 pairs at a time using ESP32-S3 PIE vector instructions
// Requirements: len must be multiple of 16, both pointers must be 16-byte aligned
static inline int32_t dotprod_s8_simd(const int8_t* a, const int8_t* b, int len) {
    int32_t result;
    int chunks = len >> 4;  // len / 16

    asm volatile(
        // Clear 40-bit accumulator (MUST do this before accumulating)
        "wur.accx_0 %[zero]\n"        // Write 0 to low 32 bits
        "wur.accx_1 %[zero]\n"        // Write 0 to high 8 bits

        // Hardware loop: process 16 int8 pairs per iteration
        "loopnez %[chunks], 1f\n"     // Loop until chunks == 0

        // Loop body (executes 'chunks' times)
        "ee.vld.128.ip q0, %[a], 16\n"    // Load 16 int8s from a[], a += 16
        "ee.vld.128.ip q1, %[b], 16\n"    // Load 16 int8s from b[], b += 16
        "ee.vmulas.s8.accx q0, q1\n"      // accx += sum(q0[i] * q1[i]) for i=0..15

        "1:\n"                            // Loop end label

        // Extract result from accumulator
        "rur.accx_0 %[result]\n"          // Read low 32 bits of accumulator

        // Output/input operand constraints
        : [result] "=r" (result),         // Output: result goes to a register
          [a] "+r" (a),                   // Input/output: a pointer (modified by vld)
          [b] "+r" (b)                    // Input/output: b pointer (modified by vld)

        // Input operands
        : [chunks] "r" (chunks),          // Input: loop count
          [zero] "r" (0)                  // Input: zero value for clearing

        // Clobbers
        : "memory"                        // Tell compiler memory may change
    );

    return result;
}
```

Let me walk through this line by line because understanding this is key to understanding the entire optimization.

### The Assembly Breakdown

**Setting up the accumulator:**
```cpp
"wur.accx_0 %[zero]\n"
"wur.accx_1 %[zero]\n"
```
Before we start accumulating, we must clear the 40-bit accumulator. It retains its value between calls, so if we forget this, we get garbage. The `%[zero]` refers to the input operand we defined as `[zero] "r" (0)` - the compiler puts 0 in a register for us.

**The hardware loop:**
```cpp
"loopnez %[chunks], 1f\n"
```
This is pure magic. Instead of:
```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < chunks; i++) {
    // decrement counter
    // compare to zero
    // conditional branch
}
```

The `loopnez` instruction tells the hardware "execute the following instructions until the count reaches zero, branching back to here automatically". The branch back is handled in hardware with zero penalty. The `1f` is a forward reference to label `1:` which marks where the loop ends.

**Loading the vectors:**
```cpp
"ee.vld.128.ip q0, %[a], 16\n"
"ee.vld.128.ip q1, %[b], 16\n"
```
Each instruction loads 128 bits (16 bytes = 16 int8 values) from memory into a vector register. The `ip` suffix means "immediate post-increment" - after loading, the pointer automatically advances by 16 bytes. This is why our input pointers need the `+r` constraint (they are modified by the instruction).

**The fused MAC:**
```cpp
"ee.vmulas.s8.accx q0, q1\n"
```
This single instruction performs 16 multiplications and 16 additions:
```
accx += q0[0]*q1[0] + q0[1]*q1[1] + ... + q0[15]*q1[15]
```

In one cycle, we are doing what would take a scalar implementation 32+ cycles (16 muls + 16 adds + memory access overhead).

**Reading the result:**
```cpp
"rur.accx_0 %[result]\n"
```
Pull the low 32 bits of the accumulator into a general-purpose register. For our use case, the result always fits in 32 bits, so we ignore accx_1.

### Compiler Constraints Explained

The cryptic constraint syntax at the end is how we communicate with the GCC inline assembly system:

- `"=r" (result)` - Output constraint: result is written to a register, then copied to the C variable
- `"+r" (a)` - Input/output constraint: pointer a is read AND modified by the assembly
- `"r" (chunks)` - Input constraint: chunks is read-only, put it in any register
- `"memory"` - Clobber: tell the compiler we might have read/written to memory

Getting these constraints wrong causes subtle bugs - the compiler might optimize away a reload it thinks is unnecessary, or fail to save a register value it assumes is preserved.

### The 16x Speedup

Let us compare to a naive scalar implementation:

```cpp
int32_t dotprod_scalar(const int8_t* a, const int8_t* b, int len) {
    int32_t sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        sum += a[i] * b[i];  // 1 mul, 1 add per iteration
    }
    return sum;
}
```

For len=64 (one quantization group):
- Scalar: 64 iterations x (load + load + mul + add) = ~256 operations
- SIMD: 4 iterations x (vld + vld + vmulas) = 12 instructions, but each vmulas does 16 ops

That is roughly 16x fewer instructions for the same work. In practice, the speedup is somewhat less due to memory bandwidth limits and instruction latencies, but we consistently see 10-15x improvement in real benchmarks.

---

## Quantized Matmul Integration

The dot product is just one piece. Here is how it integrates into the full matrix multiplication:

```cpp
void matmul_q8(float* xout, QuantizedTensor* x, QuantizedTensor* w, int n, int d) {
    // For each output element
    for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) {
        float val = 0.0f;
        int in = i * n;  // Row offset in weight matrix

        // Process each quantization group
        for (int j = 0; j <= n - GS; j += GS) {
            // SIMD dot product for this group (GS elements, typically 64)
            int32_t ival = dotprod_s8_simd(x->q + j, w->q + in + j, GS);

            // Scale by both quantization factors
            // This is the key: scales are applied ONCE per group, not per element
            val += (float)ival * w->s[(in + j) / GS] * x->s[j / GS];
        }
        xout[i] = val;
    }
}
```

### Why This Layout Works

The critical insight is keeping the int8 operations in the inner loop and floating-point scaling in the outer loop. If we dequantized every element before multiplying:

```cpp
// BAD: Dequantize first (slow!)
for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
    float a_val = x->q[j] * x->s[j / GS];      // Dequantize
    float w_val = w->q[i*n + j] * w->s[(i*n + j) / GS];  // Dequantize
    val += a_val * w_val;                        // Float multiply
}
```

We would have 2 float multiplies per element. With our approach:

```cpp
// GOOD: Quantized inner loop
int32_t ival = dotprod_s8_simd(...);  // 64 int8 muls, accumulated
val += (float)ival * scale_w * scale_x;  // Just 2 float muls per GROUP
```

We do 2 float multiplies per 64 elements instead of per element. That is 32x fewer float operations.

### Memory Alignment Requirements

Notice this line from the memory allocation code:

```cpp
// MUST be 16-byte aligned for PIE SIMD weight access
t->raw_data = (uint8_t*)heap_caps_aligned_alloc(16, t->file_size, MALLOC_CAP_SPIRAM);
```

And for activation buffers:

```cpp
s->xq.q = (int8_t*)heap_caps_aligned_alloc(16, p->dim * sizeof(int8_t), MALLOC_CAP_SPIRAM);
```

The `ee.vld.128.ip` instruction requires 16-byte aligned addresses. If you pass an unaligned pointer, you get a LoadStoreAlignment exception and the CPU halts. The `heap_caps_aligned_alloc` function guarantees our buffers start at addresses divisible by 16.

## Other SIMD Optimizations

The PIE assembly handles the quantized matmul, but we have other operations that benefit from SIMD too. For these, we use ESP-DSP library functions which are highly optimized but work with floats.

### RMSNorm with ESP-DSP

```cpp
void rmsnorm(float* o, float* x, float* weight, int size) {
    // Sum of squares using SIMD dot product
    float ss = 0.0f;
    dsps_dotprod_f32_aes3(x, x, &ss, size);  // ss = sum(x[i]^2)

    // Normalization factor: 1/sqrt(mean(x^2) + epsilon)
    ss = 1.0f / sqrtf(ss / size + 1e-5f);

    // Scale x by ss, then multiply by weight - two SIMD passes
    dsps_mulc_f32_ae32(x, o, size, ss, 1, 1);       // o = x * ss
    dsps_mul_f32_ae32(o, weight, o, size, 1, 1, 1); // o = o * weight
}
```

The `dsps_dotprod_f32_aes3` function uses the AES3 SIMD instructions (different from PIE, these work on floats). Computing `x dot x` gives us the sum of squares in one vectorized pass instead of a scalar loop.

### Softmax with Numerical Stability

```cpp
void softmax(float* x, int size) {
    // Find max for numerical stability (prevents exp overflow)
    float max_val = x[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        if (x[i] > max_val) max_val = x[i];
    }

    // Exp and sum (expf is the bottleneck, cannot SIMD this easily)
    float sum = 0.0f;
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        x[i] = expf(x[i] - max_val);  // Subtract max to prevent overflow
        sum += x[i];
    }

    // Vectorized division: multiply by 1/sum
    float inv_sum = 1.0f / sum;
    dsps_mulc_f32_ae32(x, x, size, inv_sum, 1, 1);
}
```

The `expf()` calls are the bottleneck here - transcendental functions are hard to SIMD. But we can at least vectorize the final division by converting it to multiplication by the inverse.

### Temperature Scaling in Sampler

```cpp
int sample(Sampler* sampler, float* logits) {
    if (sampler->temperature == 0.0f) {
        // Greedy: just pick the max
        return sample_argmax(logits, sampler->vocab_size);
    }

    // Temperature scaling using SIMD
    float inv_temp = 1.0f / sampler->temperature;
    dsps_mulc_f32_ae32(logits, logits, sampler->vocab_size, inv_temp, 1, 1);

    // Softmax and sample
    softmax_sampling(logits, sampler->vocab_size);
    // ... top-p sampling logic
}
```

Scaling 1024 logits by temperature would be 1024 divisions. Converting to multiplication by 1/temperature and using SIMD gives us roughly 4x speedup for this operation.

## Three-Phase Training Pipeline

Now for the other half of this story: how do we train a 6MB model to answer 2,008 specific questions? The answer is a three-phase training pipeline that progressively specializes the model.

{{< sub-section title="Why Three Phases?" icon="fa-graduation-cap" >}}
Training a tiny model on a specialized task from scratch does not work well. The model lacks the "language prior" - basic understanding of grammar, sentence structure, and semantics. By training in phases, we first establish general language ability, then gradually focus on the target domain.
{{< /sub-section >}}

### Phase 1: TinyStories (Language Foundation)

**Goal**: Learn English sentence structure, grammar, and narrative flow

**Data**: 200,000 children's stories from the TinyStories dataset

**Training**: 20,000 steps at learning rate 3e-4

**Final Loss**: 1.55

This phase teaches the model what English looks like. TinyStories are perfect because they use simple vocabulary and clear sentence structures - exactly what a tiny model can handle. After this phase, the model can generate coherent (if simple) sentences:

```
Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lucy.
She wanted to play in the garden.
```

### Phase 2: Profile Grounding (Factual Knowledge)

**Goal**: Ground the model in specific facts about a person

**Data**: 5,100 GPT-generated prose paragraphs + 2,178 synthetic Q&A pairs

**Training**: 10,000 steps at learning rate 1e-4 (lower to preserve Phase 1 knowledge)

**Final Loss**: 0.013 (yes, we want overfitting here!)

This is where it gets interesting. We used GPT-4 to extract prose paragraphs from a personal profile:

```
Alphons Jaimon's role at Etherwise involves tackling diverse challenges 
like AI-assisted trading SaaS platforms, automation scripts, and enhanced 
ChatGPT clones with RAG pipelines. With a team of just four, the 
environment demands quick adaptations...
```

We also generated synthetic Q&A pairs:
```
<|user|>What is Alphons email address<|assistant|>chat@ajv009.com<|end|>
<|user|>Does Alphons know Python<|assistant|>Yes for AI ML work<|end|>
```

The loss of 0.013 looks like severe overfitting - and it is! That is intentional. We want the model to memorize these facts, not generalize from them.

### Phase 3: Q&A Memorization (Instruction Tuning)

**Goal**: Drill the exact question-answer format into the model

**Data**: 2,008 Q&A pairs from a curated CSV, repeated 50x = 100,400 samples

**Training**: 12,000 steps at learning rate 5e-5 (very low, fine-tuning)

**Final Loss**: 0.24

This phase takes the 2,008 human-written Q&A pairs and hammers them into the model through repetition:

```csv
"What is Alphons email address","chat@ajv009.com"
"What is his phone number","+91-8237842347"
"When was Alphons born","August 2001"
"Where does he live","Maharashtra India"
"What languages does Alphons know","English Hindi Marathi Malayalam"
```

Each pair is wrapped with special tokens:
```
<|user|>What is Alphons email address<|assistant|>chat@ajv009.com<|end|>
```

The 50x repetition ensures the model sees each Q&A pair many times during training. Combined with the very low learning rate, this creates strong associations without destroying the language knowledge from Phases 1-2.

### Learning Rate Scheduling

The decreasing learning rates across phases are crucial:

| Phase | Learning Rate | Purpose |
|-------|--------------|---------|
| P1 | 3e-4 | Fast learning - model is random, big updates OK |
| P2 | 1e-4 | Moderate - preserve language, add facts |
| P3 | 5e-5 | Slow - fine-tune associations, minimal forgetting |

If we used 3e-4 in Phase 3, the model would "forget" its language abilities while memorizing Q&A. The low rate makes small adjustments that specialize without destroying.

---

## Model Scaling Options

Not every ESP32-S3 has the same constraints. Here are the model sizes we trained and their trade-offs:

| Model | Parameters | Int8 Size | Dim | Layers | Quality | Speed |
|-------|------------|-----------|-----|--------|---------|-------|
| 1M | 1.0M | 1.07 MB | 128 | 4 | Basic | Fast |
| 3M | 3.0M | 2.82 MB | 176 | 6 | Good | Medium |
| 6M | 5.6M | 5.98 MB | 224 | 8 | Best | Slower |

The model architecture scales these parameters:
- `dim`: Embedding/hidden dimension (bigger = richer representations)
- `hidden_dim`: FFN intermediate size (4x dim)
- `n_layers`: Transformer layers (more = deeper understanding)
- `n_heads`: Attention heads (fixed at 8)
- `n_kv_heads`: Key-Value heads for GQA (fixed at 4)

For our badge with 8MB PSRAM, the 6M model is tight but works:
- Model: 5.98 MB
- Token embeddings (dequantized): ~0.9 MB
- KV cache (64 seq len): ~0.5 MB
- Activation buffers: ~0.2 MB
- Total: ~7.6 MB out of 8 MB

If you have less PSRAM, the 3M model is a sweet spot - good quality, comfortable memory margins.

---

## SAM TTS Integration

Once the LLM generates text, we need to speak it. Enter SAM - the "Software Automatic Mouth" from 1982, originally for the Commodore 64. Yes, we are using 43-year-old speech synthesis technology. And it is perfect.

{{< sub-section title="Why SAM?" icon="fa-robot" >}}
Modern TTS systems like Tacotron or VITS produce human-quality speech but require gigabytes of models and GPU inference. SAM produces robotic speech with ~10KB of code. For a conference badge with limited resources and a "digital assistant" aesthetic, the robot voice is a feature, not a bug.
{{< /sub-section >}}

### Custom I2S Output Adapter

The ESP32-SAM library by pschatzmann provides the SAM engine, but we needed a custom output adapter for our I2S speaker:

```cpp
class SAMI2SOutput : public SAMOutputBase {
public:
    SAMI2SOutput(i2s_port_t port, int bclk, int lrc, int dout);

    void open() override {
        i2s_config_t i2s_config = {
            .mode = (i2s_mode_t)(I2S_MODE_MASTER | I2S_MODE_TX),
            .sample_rate = SAMOutputBase::sampleRate(),  // 22050 Hz - SAM's native rate
            .bits_per_sample = I2S_BITS_PER_SAMPLE_16BIT,
            .channel_format = I2S_CHANNEL_FMT_RIGHT_LEFT,
            .communication_format = I2S_COMM_FORMAT_STAND_I2S,
            .dma_buf_count = 8,
            .dma_buf_len = 256,
        };

        i2s_driver_install(_port, &i2s_config, 0, NULL);
        i2s_set_pin(_port, &pin_config);
    }

    bool write(byte* buffer, int bytes_count) override {
        size_t bytes_written;
        esp_err_t result = i2s_write(_port, buffer, bytes_count, 
                                      &bytes_written, portMAX_DELAY);
        return result == ESP_OK;
    }
};
```

SAM outputs 22050 Hz audio natively - a holdover from 1980s hardware capabilities. We configure I2S to match this rate exactly.

### Voice Tuning

SAM has four parameters that shape the voice character:

```cpp
void RobotTTS::setVoice(Voice voice) {
    switch (voice) {
        case ROBOT:
            // Ultra-robotic: slow, low pitch, harsh resonance
            _sam->setSpeed(100);    // Slower for dramatic effect
            _sam->setPitch(50);     // Lower pitch
            _sam->setThroat(200);   // Harsh throat resonance
            _sam->setMouth(200);    // Wide mouth resonance
            break;
    }
}
```

- **Speed**: How fast phonemes are spoken (72 = normal, 100 = slower)
- **Pitch**: Fundamental frequency (64 = normal, 50 = deeper)
- **Throat**: Throat resonance character (128 = normal, 200 = harsh)
- **Mouth**: Mouth resonance character (128 = normal, 200 = wide)

Our "ultra-robotic" settings produce a slow, deep, mechanical voice that sounds like a 1980s sci-fi computer. Hehe, exactly the vibe we wanted.

---

## Results and Benchmarks

After all this optimization, here is where we landed:

### Inference Performance

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Token generation | 1.2-1.5 tok/s |
| First token latency | ~800ms |
| Memory usage | ~7.6 MB |
| Model load time | ~3 seconds |

### Quality Assessment

For questions in the training set:
```
Q: What is the name?
A: Alphons Jaimon

Q: What is the email?
A: chat@ajv009.com

Q: Does Alphons know Python?
A: Yes for AI ML work
```

The model accurately recalls trained facts. For questions slightly outside training:
```
Q: Tell me about Alphons.
A: More about consciousness transfer and upload
```

It tries to answer but may confuse topics. This is a 6M parameter model - it does not truly "understand", it pattern-matches. The training data determines what it can answer reliably.

### What We Would Improve

1. **Larger vocabulary**: 1024 tokens is tight. Some words get split awkwardly.
2. **Better prompt engineering**: The special tokens work but could be more robust.
3. **Streaming generation**: Currently batches the full response before TTS.
4. **Model pruning**: Structured pruning could reduce size further without retraining.

---

## Closing Thoughts

Building this system was an exercise in constraints breeding creativity. When you cannot throw more compute at the problem, you have to get clever. The PIE assembly optimization alone took days of reading Espressif documentation and debugging subtle alignment issues. The training pipeline went through many iterations before finding the right phase balance.

But the result - a conference badge that listens for a wake word, understands your question, generates a personalized response, and speaks it in a robot voice, all running on a $10 microcontroller - feels like magic. Stupid, wonderful, low-tech magic.

The code is not pretty in places. The assembly is cryptic. The training pipeline is held together with duct tape and repetition counts. But it works, and it works on hardware that costs less than a fancy coffee.

That is what embedded AI is about. Not matching GPT-4, but doing something useful on hardware that fits in your pocket with a battery that lasts all day. The "100x faster matmul" in the title is not hyperbole - 16 MACs per cycle versus 1 really is a massive difference when you are doing millions of multiplies per second.

So yeah, Blog 5 turned into a deep dive. If you made it this far, thanks for reading. The next blog will cover power management and deep sleep - because what good is a fast inference engine if it drains your battery in an hour?

---

    82→            _modelData = nullptr;
    83→        }
    84→        return false;
    85→    }
    86→
    87→    _resetWindow();
    88→    _loaded = true;
    89→    // Start with extended cooldown (3 sec) to let mic stabilize and avoid false triggers
    90→    _lastDetectionMs = millis() + 1500;  // Extra 1.5s beyond normal cooldown
    91→
    92→    Serial.printf("WakeWord: Loaded \"%s\" (%.1fKB model)\n",
    93→                  _config.wake_word, _modelSize / 1024.0f);
    94→    return true;
    95→}
    96→
    97→void WakeWordDetector::end() {
    98→    // Interpreter is static, just reset pointers
    99→    _interpreter = nullptr;
   100→    _inputTensor = nullptr;
   101→    _outputTensor = nullptr;
   102→    _varAllocator = nullptr;
   103→    _resourceVars = nullptr;
   104→
   105→    if (_modelData) {
   106→        free(_modelData);
   107→        _modelData = nullptr;
   108→    }
   109→
   110→    _tensorArena = nullptr;
   111→    _varArena = nullptr;

   115→bool WakeWordDetector::_loadConfig(const char* path) {
   116→    File f = SD.open(path);
   117→    if (!f) {
   118→        return false;
   119→    }
   120→
   121→    StaticJsonDocument<512> doc;
   122→    DeserializationError error = deserializeJson(doc, f);
   123→    f.close();
   124→
   125→    if (error) {
   126→        return false;
   127→    }
   128→
   129→    // Load wake word name
   130→    const char* wake_word = doc["wake_word"] | "Hey Daisy";
   131→    strncpy(_config.wake_word, wake_word, sizeof(_config.wake_word) - 1);
   132→    _config.wake_word[sizeof(_config.wake_word) - 1] = '\0';
   133→
   134→    // Load detection parameters from "micro" object
   135→    JsonObject micro = doc["micro"];
   136→    if (micro) {
   137→        _config.probability_cutoff = micro["probability_cutoff"] | 0.5f;
   138→        _config.sliding_window_size = micro["sliding_window_average_size"] | 10;
   139→        _config.min_high_frames = micro["min_high_frames"] | 6;
   140→        _config.min_frame_prob = micro["min_frame_prob"] | 0.5f;
   141→        _config.cooldown_ms = micro["cooldown_ms"] | 1500;
   142→    }
   143→
   144→    // Clamp sliding window size
   145→    if (_config.sliding_window_size > MAX_SLIDING_WINDOW) {
   146→        _config.sliding_window_size = MAX_SLIDING_WINDOW;
   147→    }
   148→
   149→    return true;
   150→}
   151→
   152→bool WakeWordDetector::_loadModel(const char* path) {
   153→    File f = SD.open(path);
   154→    if (!f) {
   155→        Serial.printf("WakeWord: Cannot open %s\n", path);
   156→        return false;
   157→    }
   158→
   159→    _modelSize = f.size();
   160→    _modelData = (uint8_t*)ps_malloc(_modelSize);
   161→    if (!_modelData) {
   162→        Serial.println("WakeWord: Model alloc failed");
   163→        f.close();

   166→
   167→    if (f.read(_modelData, _modelSize) != _modelSize) {
   168→        free(_modelData);

   170→        f.close();
   171→        return false;
   172→    }
   173→    f.close();
   174→    return true;

   176→
   177→bool WakeWordDetector::_initInterpreter() {
   178→    const tflite::Model* model = tflite::GetModel(_modelData);
   179→    if (model->version() != TFLITE_SCHEMA_VERSION) {
   180→        Serial.printf("WakeWord: Model version mismatch: %d vs %d\n",
   181→                      model->version(), TFLITE_SCHEMA_VERSION);
   182→        return false;
   183→    }
   184→
   185→    // CRITICAL: Clear the arena to reset MicroAllocator state from any previous model
   186→    // This prevents "Model allocation started before finishing" errors
   187→    memset(_tensorArena, 0, TENSOR_ARENA_SIZE);
   188→    memset(_varArena, 0, VAR_ARENA_SIZE);
   189→
   190→    _varAllocator = tflite::MicroAllocator::Create(_varArena, VAR_ARENA_SIZE);
   191→    if (!_varAllocator) {
   192→        Serial.println("WakeWord: Var allocator failed");
   193→        return false;
   194→    }
   195→
   196→    _resourceVars = tflite::MicroResourceVariables::Create(_varAllocator, MAX_RESOURCE_VARS);
   197→    if (!_resourceVars) {
   198→        Serial.println("WakeWord: Resource vars failed");
   199→        return false;
   200→    }
   201→
   202→    // Use placement new to properly reconstruct the interpreter each time
   203→    // This ensures the constructor runs with fresh model/arena/resource vars
   204→    static uint8_t interpreterBuffer[sizeof(tflite::MicroInterpreter)] __attribute__((aligned(16)));
   205→    _interpreter = new (interpreterBuffer) tflite::MicroInterpreter(
   206→        model, resolver, _tensorArena, TENSOR_ARENA_SIZE, _resourceVars);
   207→
   208→    if (_interpreter->AllocateTensors() != kTfLiteOk) {
   209→        Serial.println("WakeWord: AllocateTensors failed");
   210→        return false;
   211→    }
   212→
   213→    _inputTensor = _interpreter->input(0);
   214→    _outputTensor = _interpreter->output(0);
   215→
   216→    if (!_inputTensor || !_outputTensor) {
   217→        Serial.println("WakeWord: Failed to get tensors");
   218→        return false;
   219→    }
   220→
   221→    return true;
   222→}
   223→
   224→float WakeWordDetector::_runInference(const uint16_t* features) {
   225→    int total_features = FEATURE_FRAMES * FEATURE_BINS;
   226→
   227→    // Quantize features to input tensor format
   228→    if (_inputTensor->type == kTfLiteInt8) {
   229→        int8_t* input_data = _inputTensor->data.int8;
   230→        for (int i = 0; i < total_features; i++) {
   231→            int32_t scaled = ((int32_t)features[i] * 256 + 333) / 666 - 128;
   232→            input_data[i] = constrain(scaled, -128, 127);
   233→        }
   234→    } else {
   235→        // Float input
   236→        float* input_data = _inputTensor->data.f;
   237→        for (int i = 0; i < total_features; i++) {
   238→            input_data[i] = features[i] / 25.6f;
   239→        }
   240→    }
   241→
   242→    // Run inference
   243→    if (_interpreter->Invoke() != kTfLiteOk) {
   244→        return 0.0f;
   245→    }
   246→
   247→    // Dequantize output
   248→    float probability;
   249→    if (_outputTensor->type == kTfLiteUInt8) {
   250→        uint8_t output_value = _outputTensor->data.uint8[0];
   251→        probability = (output_value - _outputTensor->params.zero_point) *
   252→                      _outputTensor->params.scale;
   253→    } else if (_outputTensor->type == kTfLiteInt8) {
   254→        int8_t output_value = _outputTensor->data.int8[0];
   255→        probability = (output_value - _outputTensor->params.zero_point) *
   256→                      _outputTensor->params.scale;
   257→    } else {
   258→        probability = _outputTensor->data.f[0];
   259→    }
   260→
   261→    return probability;
   262→}
   263→
   264→bool WakeWordDetector::detect(const uint16_t* features) {
   265→    if (!_loaded) return false;
   266→
   267→    // Run inference
   268→    float prob = _runInference(features);
   269→    _lastProbability = prob;
   270→
   271→    // Update sliding window
   272→    _probabilityWindow[_windowPos] = prob;
   273→    _windowPos = (_windowPos + 1) % _config.sliding_window_size;
   274→
   275→    if (_windowPos == 0) {
   276→        _windowFilled = true;
   277→    }
   278→
   279→    // Need full window before detection
   280→    if (!_windowFilled) {
   281→        return false;
   282→    }
   283→
   284→    // Check cooldown
   285→    if (millis() - _lastDetectionMs < (unsigned long)_config.cooldown_ms) {
   286→        return false;
   287→    }
   288→
   289→    // Calculate average and count high frames
   290→    float avg = 0.0f;
   291→    int high_frames = 0;
   292→    for (int i = 0; i < _config.sliding_window_size; i++) {
   293→        avg += _probabilityWindow[i];
   294→        if (_probabilityWindow[i] >= _config.min_frame_prob) {
   295→            high_frames++;
   296→        }
   297→    }
   298→    avg /= _config.sliding_window_size;
   299→
   300→    // Detection criteria
   301→    if (avg >= _config.probability_cutoff && high_frames >= _config.min_high_frames) {
   302→        _lastDetectionMs = millis();
   303→        _resetWindow();
   304→        return true;
   305→    }
   306→
   307→    return false;
   308→}
   309→
   310→float WakeWordDetector::getAverageProbability() const {
   311→    if (!_windowFilled) return 0.0f;
   312→
   313→    float sum = 0.0f;
   314→    for (int i = 0; i < _config.sliding_window_size; i++) {
   315→        sum += _probabilityWindow[i];
   316→    }
   317→    return sum / _config.sliding_window_size;
   318→}
   319→
   320→void WakeWordDetector::_resetWindow() {
   321→    for (int i = 0; i < MAX_SLIDING_WINDOW; i++) {
   322→        _probabilityWindow[i] = 0.0f;
   323→    }
   324→    _windowPos = 0;
   325→    _windowFilled = false;
   326→}

     1→// llm_core.cpp - Int8 Quantized LLM Inference for ESP32-S3
     2→// Based on llama2.c/runq.c - Single-core, adaptive to any model size
     3→
     4→#include "llm_core.h"
     5→#include <math.h>
     6→#include <string.h>
     7→#include <esp_heap_caps.h>  // For heap_caps_aligned_alloc (16-byte aligned SIMD buffers)
     8→
     9→// Global group size (read from model header, typically 32 or 64)
    10→int GS = 64;
    11→
    12→// ============================================================================
    13→// Quantization Functions
    14→// ============================================================================
    15→
    16→void dequantize(QuantizedTensor *qx, float* x, int n) {
    17→    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    18→        x[i] = qx->q[i] * qx->s[i / GS];
    19→    }
    20→}
    21→
    22→void quantize(QuantizedTensor *qx, float* x, int n) {
    23→    int num_groups = n / GS;
    24→    float Q_MAX = 127.0f;
    25→
    26→    for (int group = 0; group < num_groups; group++) {
    27→        float* gx = x + group * GS;
    28→        int8_t* gq = qx->q + group * GS;
    29→
    30→        // Find max absolute value using SIMD dot product trick:
    31→        // max(|x|) ≈ sqrt(max element of x²) but that's expensive
    32→        // Instead, unroll the loop for better pipelining
    33→        float wmax = 0.0f;
    34→        for (int i = 0; i < GS; i += 4) {
    35→            float v0 = fabsf(gx[i]);
    36→            float v1 = fabsf(gx[i+1]);
    37→            float v2 = fabsf(gx[i+2]);
    38→            float v3 = fabsf(gx[i+3]);
    39→            if (v0 > wmax) wmax = v0;
    40→            if (v1 > wmax) wmax = v1;
    41→            if (v2 > wmax) wmax = v2;
    42→            if (v3 > wmax) wmax = v3;
    43→        }
    44→
    45→        float scale = wmax / Q_MAX;
    46→        qx->s[group] = scale;
    47→
    48→        // Quantize with reciprocal multiply (faster than division)
    49→        float inv_scale = (scale > 1e-10f) ? Q_MAX / wmax : 0.0f;
    50→        for (int i = 0; i < GS; i += 4) {
    51→            gq[i]   = (int8_t)(gx[i]   * inv_scale + 0.5f - (gx[i]   < 0));
    52→            gq[i+1] = (int8_t)(gx[i+1] * inv_scale + 0.5f - (gx[i+1] < 0));
    53→            gq[i+2] = (int8_t)(gx[i+2] * inv_scale + 0.5f - (gx[i+2] < 0));
    54→            gq[i+3] = (int8_t)(gx[i+3] * inv_scale + 0.5f - (gx[i+3] < 0));
    55→        }
    56→    }
    57→}
    58→
    59→// ============================================================================
    60→// Neural Network Operations
    61→// ============================================================================
    62→
    63→void rmsnorm(float* o, float* x, float* weight, int size) {
    64→    // Sum of squares using SIMD dot product
    65→    float ss = 0.0f;
    66→    dsps_dotprod_f32_aes3(x, x, &ss, size);
    67→
    68→    // Normalization factor
    69→    ss = 1.0f / sqrtf(ss / size + 1e-5f);
    70→
    71→    // Scale x by ss, then multiply by weight
    72→    // o[i] = weight[i] * (ss * x[i])
    73→    dsps_mulc_f32_ae32(x, o, size, ss, 1, 1);       // o = x * ss
    74→    dsps_mul_f32_ae32(o, weight, o, size, 1, 1, 1); // o = o * weight
    75→}
    76→
    77→void softmax(float* x, int size) {
    78→    // Find max (no SIMD equivalent that's faster for small arrays)
    79→    float max_val = x[0];
    80→    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
    81→        if (x[i] > max_val) max_val = x[i];
    82→    }
    83→
    84→    // Exp and sum (expf() is the bottleneck, can't SIMD this)
    85→    float sum = 0.0f;
    86→    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
    87→        x[i] = expf(x[i] - max_val);
    88→        sum += x[i];
    89→    }
    90→
    91→    // Vectorized division using SIMD multiply by inverse
    92→    float inv_sum = 1.0f / sum;
    93→    dsps_mulc_f32_ae32(x, x, size, inv_sum, 1, 1);
    94→}
    95→
    96→// PIE SIMD int8 dot product - returns full int32 accumulator
    97→// Processes 16 int8 pairs at a time using ESP32-S3 PIE vector instructions
    98→// Requirements: len must be multiple of 16, both pointers must be 16-byte aligned
    99→static inline int32_t dotprod_s8_simd(const int8_t* a, const int8_t* b, int len) {
   100→    int32_t result;
   101→    int chunks = len >> 4;  // len / 16
   102→
   103→    asm volatile(
   104→        // Clear 40-bit accumulator
   105→        "wur.accx_0 %[zero]\n"
   106→        "wur.accx_1 %[zero]\n"
   107→
   108→        // Process 16 int8 pairs per iteration
   109→        "loopnez %[chunks], 1f\n"
   110→        "ee.vld.128.ip q0, %[a], 16\n"    // Load 16 int8s from a
   111→        "ee.vld.128.ip q1, %[b], 16\n"    // Load 16 int8s from b
   112→        "ee.vmulas.s8.accx q0, q1\n"      // MAC: accx += sum(q0[i] * q1[i])
   113→        "1:\n"
   114→
   115→        // Read low 32 bits of accumulator
   116→        "rur.accx_0 %[result]\n"
   117→
   118→        : [result] "=r" (result), [a] "+r" (a), [b] "+r" (b)
   119→        : [chunks] "r" (chunks), [zero] "r" (0)
   120→        : "memory"
   121→    );
   122→
   123→    return result;
   124→}
   125→
   126→void matmul_q8(float* xout, QuantizedTensor* x, QuantizedTensor* w, int n, int d) {
   127→    for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) {
   128→        float val = 0.0f;
   129→        int in = i * n;
   130→
   131→        // Process each quantization group with SIMD
   132→        for (int j = 0; j <= n - GS; j += GS) {
   133→            // SIMD dot product for this group (GS elements)
   134→            int32_t ival = dotprod_s8_simd(x->q + j, w->q + in + j, GS);
   135→
   136→            // Scale by quantization scales
   137→            val += (float)ival * w->s[(in + j) / GS] * x->s[j / GS];
   138→        }
   139→        xout[i] = val;
   140→    }
   141→}

   147→static bool malloc_run_state(RunState* s, Config* p) {
   148→    int kv_dim = (p->dim * p->n_kv_heads) / p->n_heads;
   149→
   150→    size_t kv_cache_size = (size_t)p->n_layers * p->seq_len * kv_dim * sizeof(float);
   151→    size_t total_needed =
   152→        3 * p->dim * sizeof(float) +
   153→        2 * p->hidden_dim * sizeof(float) +
   154→        p->dim * sizeof(float) +
   155→        p->n_heads * p->seq_len * sizeof(float) +
   156→        p->vocab_size * sizeof(float) +
   157→        2 * kv_cache_size +
   158→        p->dim + p->dim / GS * sizeof(float) +
   159→        p->hidden_dim + p->hidden_dim / GS * sizeof(float);
   160→
   161→    Serial.printf("RunState: need %dKB, free %dKB, kv_dim=%d, hidden=%d\n",
   162→                  total_needed / 1024, ESP.getFreePsram() / 1024,
   163→                  kv_dim, p->hidden_dim);
   164→
   165→    if (total_needed > ESP.getFreePsram()) {
   166→        Serial.println("ERROR: Not enough PSRAM for RunState!");
   167→        return false;
   168→    }
   169→
   170→    s->x = (float*)ps_calloc(p->dim, sizeof(float));
   171→    s->xb = (float*)ps_calloc(p->dim, sizeof(float));
   172→    s->xb2 = (float*)ps_calloc(p->dim, sizeof(float));
   173→    s->hb = (float*)ps_calloc(p->hidden_dim, sizeof(float));
   174→    s->hb2 = (float*)ps_calloc(p->hidden_dim, sizeof(float));
   175→    s->q = (float*)ps_calloc(p->dim, sizeof(float));
   176→    s->att = (float*)ps_calloc(p->n_heads * p->seq_len, sizeof(float));
   177→    s->logits = (float*)ps_calloc(p->vocab_size, sizeof(float));
   178→
   179→    s->key_cache = (float*)ps_calloc(p->n_layers * p->seq_len * kv_dim, sizeof(float));
   180→    s->value_cache = (float*)ps_calloc(p->n_layers * p->seq_len * kv_dim, sizeof(float));
   181→
   182→    // Quantized activation buffers - MUST be 16-byte aligned for PIE SIMD
   183→    s->xq.q = (int8_t*)heap_caps_aligned_alloc(16, p->dim * sizeof(int8_t), MALLOC_CAP_SPIRAM);
   184→    s->xq.s = (float*)ps_calloc(p->dim / GS, sizeof(float));
   185→    s->hq.q = (int8_t*)heap_caps_aligned_alloc(16, p->hidden_dim * sizeof(int8_t), MALLOC_CAP_SPIRAM);
   186→    s->hq.s = (float*)ps_calloc(p->hidden_dim / GS, sizeof(float));
   187→
   188→    // Debug: check which allocation failed
   189→    if (!s->x) Serial.println("  x alloc failed");
   190→    if (!s->xb) Serial.println("  xb alloc failed");
   191→    if (!s->xb2) Serial.println("  xb2 alloc failed");
   192→    if (!s->hb) Serial.println("  hb alloc failed");
   193→    if (!s->hb2) Serial.println("  hb2 alloc failed");
   194→    if (!s->q) Serial.println("  q alloc failed");
   195→    if (!s->att) Serial.println("  att alloc failed");
   196→    if (!s->logits) Serial.println("  logits alloc failed");
   197→    if (!s->key_cache) Serial.println("  key_cache alloc failed");
   198→    if (!s->value_cache) Serial.println("  value_cache alloc failed");
   199→    if (!s->xq.q) Serial.println("  xq.q alloc failed");
   200→    if (!s->xq.s) Serial.println("  xq.s alloc failed");
   201→    if (!s->hq.q) Serial.println("  hq.q alloc failed");
   202→    if (!s->hq.s) Serial.println("  hq.s alloc failed");
   203→
   204→    if (!s->x || !s->xb || !s->xb2 || !s->hb || !s->hb2 || !s->q ||
   205→        !s->att || !s->logits || !s->key_cache || !s->value_cache ||
   206→        !s->xq.q || !s->xq.s || !s->hq.q || !s->hq.s) {
   207→        Serial.printf("RunState: PSRAM after failed allocs: %dKB\n", ESP.getFreePsram() / 1024);
   208→        Serial.println("ERROR: RunState allocation failed!");
   209→        return false;
   210→    }
   211→
   212→    return true;
   213→}
